public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 871

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/871](https://www.erdosproblems.com/871)
- [ErNa88] Erdős, Paul and Nathanson, Melvyn B., *Partitions of bases into disjoint unions of bases*. J. Number Theory (1988), 1-9.
- [ErNa89] Erdős, Paul and Nathanson, Melvyn B., *Additive bases with many representations*. Acta Arith. (1989), 399-406.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos871

/--
Let $A$ be an additive basis of order $2$, and suppose $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. Can $A$ be partitioned into two disjoint additive bases of order $2$?

A question of Erdős and Nathanson [ErNa88], who proved this is true if $1_A\ast 1_A(n) > c\log n$ (for all large $n$) for some constant $c>(\log\frac{4}{3})^{-1}$. Erdős and Nathanson [ErNa89] also proved that for every $t$ there exists a basis $A$ of order $2$ such that $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\geq t$ for all large $n$ and yet $A$ cannot be partitioned into two disjoint additive bases. This has been disproved by Larsen using Claude Opus 4.5 - in fact only a small modification of the argument of [ErNa89] is required.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos871.lean"]
theorem erdos_871 :
    answer(False) ↔
      ∀ (A : Set ℕ),
        (∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, a + b = n) ∧
        (∀ t, ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, ∃ pairs : Finset (ℕ × ℕ),
          pairs.card ≥ t ∧
            ∀ p ∈ pairs, p.1 ∈ A ∧ p.2 ∈ A ∧ p.1 + p.2 = n ∧ p.1 ≤ p.2) →
        ∃ (B C : Set ℕ),
          (∀ x, x ∈ A ↔ x ∈ B ∨ x ∈ C) ∧
          Disjoint B C ∧
          (∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, ∃ a ∈ B, ∃ b ∈ B, a + b = n) ∧
          (∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, ∃ a ∈ C, ∃ b ∈ C, a + b = n) := by
  sorry

end Erdos871

reformulations.difference: The source's hypothesis `1_A∗1_A(n) → ∞` counts ordered pairs. The Lean states it as `∀ t, ∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∃ pairs : Finset (ℕ × ℕ), pairs.card ≥ t ∧ ∀ p ∈ pairs, p.1 ∈ A ∧ p.2 ∈ A ∧ p.1 + p.2 = n ∧ p.1 ≤ p.2`, i.e. the unordered count r_A(n) = #{(a,b) : a ≤ b} tends to infinity via a Finset witness. The additive-basis conditions are written out explicitly (`∀ᶠ n in atTop, ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, a + b = n`) instead of using `Set.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2`. The first conjunct is also redundant.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Write O(n) for the ordered count and U(n) for the unordered count. Then U(n) ≤ O(n) ≤ 2·U(n), because the ordered pairs lie in U ∪ swap(U). So O → ∞ iff U → ∞. A Finset of distinct valid pairs has card ≤ U(n), and the filtered antidiagonal is such a Finset with card exactly U(n). So '∀ t, eventually some Finset of ≥ t valid pairs exists' iff U(n) → ∞. Proved in Lean (scratch file): `pairs_iff` shows the Lean condition ↔ `Tendsto (fun n => #{p ∈ antidiagonal n | p.1 ∈ A ∧ p.2 ∈ A}) atTop atTop`. `basis_iff` shows the explicit basis condition ↔ `A.IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2`. `restated` shows the whole right-hand side ↔ '∀ A, IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2 → ordered count → ∞ → ∃ B C, B ∪ C = A ∧ Disjoint B C ∧ both IsAsymptoticAddBasisOfOrder 2'. `pairs_imp_basis` shows the first conjunct follows from the second. The unordered count with a ≤ b is exactly Erdős–Nathanson's r_A(n) (zbMATH review of ErNa89) and Nathanson's r_{2,A}(n).

reformulations.difference: The Lean reads 'additive basis of order 2' as 'A + A contains all sufficiently large integers' (exactly two summands) for A, B and C. The erdosproblems.com definitions page defines 'additive basis of order k' as 'all sufficiently large integers are the sum of at most k integers from A'. Under that reading the partition conclusion would only need every large n ∈ B ∪ (B+B) and n ∈ C ∪ (C+C), which is formally weaker.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The exactly-two notion is the one used by the original source: ErNa88 and ErNa89 per their zbMATH reviews ('{a+b : a,b ∈ A} ⊇ [n₀,∞) ∩ ℕ₀'), Nathanson's survey arXiv:2310.18277 ('hA contains all sufficiently large integers'), Larsen's paper, and the site's own text for sibling problem #869 ('A_i+A_i contains all large integers'). Even so, the two readings give equivalent right-hand sides. The hypotheses coincide, since 1_A∗1_A → ∞ forces A + A ⊇ all large integers. Both conclusions fail for Larsen's set A = B ∪ ⋃ G_k: its bad integers N_k = 2n_k+1 are not in A, since B_k ⊆ [N_{k−1}+1, n_k+N_{k−1}] and G_k ⊆ (N_k−N_{k−1}, N_k). So 'N_k ∈ B' ∪ 2B'' already forces N_k ∈ 2B', and the pigeonhole argument goes through unchanged. Checked in Lean on top of plby's construction (compiled against this repo's Mathlib): I added `Nk_not_inA`, `non_decomposable_atMost` and `fc_statement_atMost : False ↔ (at-most-2 version of the RHS)`, alongside `fc_statement : False ↔ (the file's RHS)`. Both use only the standard axioms. Both sides are therefore False, and the ↔ holds.

review.notes:
The file has a single declaration, `Erdos871.erdos_871`. Its docstring matches the erdosproblems.com LaTeX source word for word. The category `research solved` with `answer(False)` and the plby `formal_proof` link matches the site's 'DISPROVED (LEAN)' status (Larsen with Claude Opus 4.5, Jan 2026; teorth database 'disproved (Lean)', 2026-01-05).

I compiled plby's `not_erdos_871` (src/latest) against this repository's Mathlib (v4.33.1). It checks in about 40 s, and I derived from it the file's exact statement `False ↔ ∀ A, … → ∃ B C, …`, with axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] only. So the fixed `answer(False)` is machine-verified for the right-hand side as written.

Boundary checks:
- The hypotheses are satisfiable (A = ℕ), so the statement is not vacuous.
- Refuting the right-hand side needs a genuine counterexample, so the statement is not trivially provable.
- `∧` binds tighter than `→`, so the statement parses as intended (confirmed with `#print`).
- `Set ℕ` including 0 matches the sources' ℕ₀ convention (ErNa89 review 'A ⊆ ℕ₀'; Nathanson's survey 'set of nonnegative integers'; Larsen). The positive-integer version would be equivalent anyway: removing 0 from a counterexample keeps it a counterexample.

I could not read the scanned ErNa88/ErNa89 PDFs directly (image-only, no OCR tool in the sandbox). Their definitions and results were confirmed through the zbMATH reviews, Nathanson's survey and the forum discussion.
